# Analysis diagrams

## Start with meaning
Identify the question, audience, scope, source artifact/version, and evidence status. List entities, relationships, direction, labels, and important exceptions. Resolve contradictions in the model before improving presentation.

## Select a visual
| Question | Useful visual |
|---|---|
| Who handles each step? | Swimlane |
| What states and transitions are permitted? | State machine |
| Who sends what, and when? | Sequence |
| How are information entities related? | Entity relationship |
| What depends on this change? | Dependency graph |
| Who owns or receives work? | Responsibility map |
| What may cause this observed problem? | Fishbone, with hypotheses labelled |

## Preferred implementation
Use the separately installed **diagram-design** skill from https://github.com/cathrynlavery/diagram-design. Load its entrypoint and the relevant type reference. Follow the user's project style and upstream layout/accessibility checks. Default to HTML with inline SVG when appropriate; create a README-friendly image when that is the destination.

If the optional skill is unavailable, produce a clear model brief and either an explicitly requested alternative format or a simple accessible HTML/SVG draft. State which render/semantic checks were performed. Do not claim an upstream helper ran when it was unavailable.

## Preserve fidelity
Keep as-is and to-be views distinct. Do not invent a component or relationship to balance layout. If complexity requires splitting the model, provide an overview plus detail and a short ledger of merged, omitted, or deferred elements. Preserve guards, cardinalities, failure paths, and ownership when they affect the decision.

## Deliver
Return source and requested viewable artifact, a text description, source/ID mapping, assumptions, omissions, and validation performed. A polished visual does not establish the truth of its model. If a notation's formal conformance is required, use its published rules and report the scope of verification.

## Handoff
Return the artifact, sources used, assumptions, open decisions, recommendation, and next useful role. Use only available tools and authorized actions. Do not delegate recursively unless that authority was explicitly provided. Unavailable access limits evidence; it does not justify inventing it.
